loop.description: The loop's name. One document per loop; `---` separates loops in a group.

runs.description: How often the loop runs — `weekly`, `every 6 hours`, `per_question`. Free text, since cadence is domain-specific; the linter checks that one exists, not its units.

goal.description: What the loop is steering, and toward what.

beliefs.description: What it holds a view on but cannot read off directly.

when.description: The rule choosing among actions, evaluated in order. Structured rather than prose: prose reads better and cannot be checked, and the checking is the point.

asks_human_when.description: The conditions under which the loop stops and asks a person. Top-level and on its own, because burying escalation inside the decision rule is how it goes missing — this is the list a reader scans first to find out whether the thing can run away.

people.description: Who is involved — human or agent — and what each stands to lose.

never.description: Hard limits that hold regardless of the goal.

not_modelling.description: Knowingly out of scope. Not decoration: this is the first list to revisit when the loop misbehaves for reasons it cannot see.

name.description: The loop's name. One document per loop; `---` separates loops in a group.

every.description: How often the loop runs — `weekly`, `every 6 hours`, `per_question`. Free text, since cadence is domain-specific; the linter checks that one exists, not its units.

regulates.description: What the loop is steering, and toward what.

estimates.description: What it holds a view on but cannot read off directly.

parties.description: Who is involved — human or agent — and what each stands to lose.

ignoring.description: Knowingly out of scope. Not decoration: this is the first list to revisit when the loop misbehaves for reasons it cannot see.

keep.description: The target, read as a sentence: `keep: below 400`, `keep: above 3 sources`.

from.description: What this quantity is computed from.

unit.description: USD, days, percent — whatever makes the number meaningful.

confidence.description: How firmly the goal ITSELF is held, 0–1 — uncertainty about what you want, as distinct from uncertainty about the world. Optional, and deliberately not a primitive: it enters on one book sketch and that is not enough evidence.

question.description: The belief in plain language, as the question it answers — "will the customers we buy this month stay?". Optional and worth writing: it is the line a reader understands first, and the one that exposes a belief nobody can actually state.

from.description: Which observations feed this. Each must appear in `observes`.

how.description: How the view is formed: bayesian, judgement, a formula, an LLM call.

checked_by.description: What scores this belief's PAST calls against what actually happened. Its absence is the most common defect in real loops — found in three independent systems by three careful authors. A belief nothing checks cannot be shown to track anything.

explains.description: The quantity this belief is a model OF. A loop steering something it has no model of is a reflex against a setpoint — it can correct but never anticipate.

settled_by.description: The observation that would finally decide this — what makes the belief refutable.

known_bias.description: The direction this belief is expected to be wrong in, and why.

safe_to_repeat.description: What makes re-running the update safe. Execution is at-least-once on every durable runtime, and an update applied twice double-counts into a confident wrong answer.

informs.description: Which belief or goal this tells you about. Omit and it is data nobody uses.

origin.description: Did something OUTSIDE this system cause this data to exist, or did we? Half of provenance, and the half that decides whether the loop can be surprised. A loop whose every input has `origin: ourselves` is sealed — it can only agree with itself.

how.description: The other half, and orthogonal to `origin` — measured by a mechanism, reported by someone with interests, or derived from other numbers. The two axes must stay separate: `origin: ourselves` + `how: reported` is an agent's own self-assessment, which is a claim and not a measurement, and collapsing provenance to one axis cannot say it.

reported_by.description: Who reports it, when `how: reported`. A reported number is a claim by someone.

produced_by.description: Which of our own actions creates this, when `origin: ourselves`.

moves.description: The quantity this drives. Nothing pointing at a goal makes that goal a wish.

can_undo.description: THE LOAD-BEARING FIELD, phrased as the question anyone would actually ask. Approval demanded everywhere gets ignored; approval demanded where the answer is `no` is a rule people follow. `costly` means undoable at real expense. NOTE: YAML 1.1 reads bare yes/no as booleans, so `can_undo: no` arrives as False. That is accepted and normalised rather than rejected — the natural phrasing must not be a trap. It is the one place this format tolerates YAML's ambiguity, because the blind test showed people write exactly this.

needs_approval.description: The person who must say yes first. Must name someone in `people`.

effect_after.description: How long until the effect is visible. Lag with no damping is what makes loops thrash.

do.description: Action(s) to take. Must name entries in `actions`.

escalate.description: Person to ask instead. Must name someone in `people`.

agent.description: An automated actor. Mutually exclusive with `human`.

loses_if_wrong.description: What this one actually loses when the loop is wrong. `nothing` is a legitimate and revealing answer — an agent that loses nothing beside a human who loses everything is the asymmetry that explains overrides looking irrational against the agent's objective.

sees.description: What information actually reaches them. Someone who loses something and sees nothing is accountable and blind, which is oversight in name only.

may_decide.description: What this person has authority over.
